Issued at 1257 AM EDT Sun Sep 6 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Retrograding closed low pressure within a longwave troughing regime 
over Atlantic Canada has forced a large area of Canadian high 
pressure over the upper Great Lakes as a stout 500mb ridge axis 
folds overhead from the west. Result is a dry airmass over head 
that, owing to the stagnant nature of the pattern the next few days, 
will lead to continuity of abnormally warm (highs 73 to 85 through 
midweek) but still seasonable daytime highs to linger. Minimal 
sensible weather anticipated across the region owing to the 
influences of aforementioned surface high pressure. Drier air across 
the region will allow for quality diurnal temperature swings... with 
overnight lows likely dipping well into the 40s across the interior 
cold spots once again tonight, perhaps mid 50s along the more marine 
influenced coastal regions. 

Meanwhile, longwave troughing over the Pacific NW will lead to 
another shortwave crashing ashore in that region, cresting the 500mb 
ridge over the center part of the country. This wave will be quite 
juiced as it ejects into the Dakotas / Canadian Prairies, with 
surface cyclogenesis response (likely sub 1000mb) and occlusion 
manifesting by the time it gets to northern Ontario. SW return flow 
ahead of the system will lead to increasing moisture / dewpoints 
across the area into Tuesday as the system's associated occluded / 
cold frontal boundary is forced into the Great Lakes region later 
Tuesday into Wednesday. Considering potential moisture influences 
from eastern Pacific Hurricane Marie within this system, no surprise 
guidance PWAT values continue showcasing a spike in the +3.0 to +3.5 
sigma range, representing a high-end statistically significant 
anomaly compared to climatological norms. As is always the case... 
this moisture must coincide with best lift and instability within 
the atmospheric profile to generate appreciable rainfall on a 
widespread scale... otherwise the bane of my existence materializes, 
and we turn obnoxiously humid for absolutely no good reason, and 
little to nothing happens when some of the variables fail to align.

At this juncture, current models prog the passage of the boundary in 
the Tuesday evening - Wednesday night timeframe. Certainly a lot may 
change between now and then... but potential for scattered 
torrential rainfall rate outbursts is slowly creeping up. In laymans 
terms, that was a lot of meteorological jargon just to say "the next 
shower and thunder chances build from NW to SE through the late 
afternoon Tuesday through Wednesday morning... with some potential 
for heavy rainfall and to a lesser extent, severe storms". As such, 
may need to see how much of a hydrologic impact this has considering 
recent rainfalls in portions of NW lower, and portions of the region 
still contending with high soil moisture content from what has 
statistically been the wettest year to date in several areas. 

One other caveat to add to this... continuing the theme from the 
previous forecaster's thoughts... this system will come with a 
pretty well-pinched pressure gradient between the broad, deepening 
surface low to our NW and the surface high to our east. Result will 
be quite the uptick in SW winds on Tuesday, flipping more westerly 
in the dry slot behind the front. Most efficient mixing is 
anticipated within aforementioned dry slot, with winds likely 
gusting well over 30mph Wednesday, probably higher in the Straits 
and NW lower. Not looking like any land-based wind headlines in 
order for this, but certainly marine related headlines are all but 
guaranteed starting Tuesday.  

Following the passage of the frontal boundary through our neck of 
the woods, anticipation is that it stalls to our south owing to 
zonal flow building into the region as the ridge flattens from the 
wave. Result will be cooler weather building into the region 
Thursday through the end of the forecast period, but it doesn't look 
like deeper moisture will entirely scour out, so it looks like there 
may be an element of unsettled-ness that may fester as well, 
particularly as we head into the weekend. Certainly not looking like 
any washouts and plenty of dry time... just not completely dry. 
Should be noted that daytime highs moderate from a range of low 60s 
to 75 Thursday to 70 to 80 by the weekend.
